blocks.text: A graph is a set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges.
Graph algorithms are methods to traverse, search, or find shortest paths in these graphs. They power Google Maps, social networks, network routing, and GPS systems.

blocks.text: You already know BFS finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs it counts hops.
But real-world graphs have weights road distances, travel times, network latencies. BFS ignores those weights entirely.
Shortest path algorithms for weighted graphs are more nuanced.
The right choice depends on your graph:

items: Are weights positive?
Can they be negative?
Do you need one source or all pairs?

blocks.text: The four algorithms every engineer must know.
BFS explores a graph level by level it visits all neighbors of the starting node first, then their neighbors, and so on.
It uses a Queue (FIFO) to track which node to visit next. Think of it like a stone in water ripples spread outward one level at a time.
It finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph, checks if a path exists between two nodes, and explores all reachable nodes.
Data Structure to use: Queue because we process nodes in First In, First Out order.

items: First, BFS visits all nodes at distance 1 → (2, 3, 4)
Then nodes at distance 2 → (5, 6, 7, 8, 9)
Then nodes at distance 3 → (10, 11, 12)
Start at source, distance = 0
Visit all neighbors at distance 1 → then distance 2 → then distance 3…
Uses a queue (FIFO) first in, first out
Every node visited exactly once
→ Dequeue 1 → visit neighbors 2,3,4 → Queue: [2,3,4]
→ Dequeue 2 → visit neighbors 5,6 → Queue: [3,4,5,6]
→ Dequeue 3 → visit neighbor 7 → Queue: [4,5,6,7]
→ Dequeue 4 → visit neighbors 8,9 → Queue: [5,6,7,8,9]
→ Dequeue 5 → visit neighbors 10,11 → Queue: [6,7,8,9,10,11]
→ Dequeue 6 → no new neighbors → Queue: [7,8,9,10,11]
→ Dequeue 7 → visit neighbor 12 → Queue: [8,9,10,11,12]
→ Dequeue 8,9,10,11,12 → no new nodes → Queue: [] ✓ Done
Time: O(V + E) V = vertices, E = edges. Every node and edge is processed once.
Space: O(V) the queue can store nodes level by level.

blocks.text: Use BFS when you need the shortest path in an unweighted graph (all edges have same cost).

items: Social network degrees of separation
Web crawlers exploring pages level by level
Finding minimum moves in puzzles (maze, Rubik’s cube)
Simple GPS maps where all roads have equal cost

blocks.text: Do NOT use BFS when edges have different weights (use Dijkstra), or when you only need to check connectivity (DFS can be simpler).Steps to implement BFS:

items: Create a visited set and a queue, add the start node to both.
While the queue is not empty: dequeue a node, process it, then enqueue all unvisited neighbors and mark them visited.
Repeat until the queue is empty.

blocks.text: Dijkstra’s algorithm finds the shortest path from one starting node to all other nodes in a graph with non-negative weights.
It always picks the closest unvisited node first (greedy approach). Think of it like water spreading, always taking the shortest route first.
It calculates the minimum cost to reach every node from the start. You can also stop early if you only need one destination.
Data Structure to use: Min-Heap (Priority Queue) always gives the node with the smallest distance first.

items: With heap: O((V + E) log V)
Without heap: O(V²)

blocks.text: The graph shows edge weights. Starting from node A, the algorithm always picks the cheapest path next. Distances get updated step by step.

items: Round 1: Settle A=0 → relax neighbors → B=4, C=2
Round 2: Settle C=2 (smallest) → relax → E=7 (via C), F=8
Round 3: Settle B=4 → relax → D=7, E=5 (updated — shorter!)
Round 4: Settle E=5 → relax → G=8, H=9
Round 5: Settle D=7 → relax → G=9 (not better, G stays 8)
Round 6: Settle F=8, G=8 → relax → H=9 (no improvement)
Round 7: Settle H=9
A = 0 → push to heap → pop A → relax B = 4, C = 2
Pop C (min = 2) → relax E = 2 + 5 = 7, F = 2 + 6 = 8
Pop B (min = 4) → relax D = 4 + 3 = 7, E = 4 + 1 = 5 ← shorter, update
Pop E (min = 5) → relax G = 5 + 3 = 8, H = 5 + 4 = 9
Pop D (7), F (8), G (8) → no improvements
Pop H (9) → done
Time: O((V + E) log V) with a min-heap, O(V²) with a simple array
Space: O(V) to store distances and the priority queue

blocks.text: The key idea is relaxation when you reach a node, check if going through it gives a shorter path to its neighbors. If yes, update their distance.
Use Dijkstra when you have a weighted graph (non-negative weights) and need the shortest path from one source.

items: GPS and maps (Google Maps, Waze)
Network routing (OSPF)
Game pathfinding
Finding cheapest flight routes

blocks.text: Do NOT use Dijkstra when the graph has negative weights it gives wrong answers. Use Bellman-Ford instead.

items: Set all distances to infinity except the start node (distance = 0).
Push the start node into a min-heap as (0, start).
Pop the smallest distance node from the heap, skip if already finalized.
For each neighbor, calculate new_dist = current + edge_weight. If it's smaller than the known distance, update and push to heap.
Repeat until the heap is empty.

blocks.text: Finds the shortest paths between every pair of nodes in a graph. Works for directed/undirected graphs and allows negative weights (but no negative cycles).
Creates a distance matrix where dist[i][j] is the shortest distance from i to j, and keeps improving it by trying every node as an intermediate stop.
Data Structure to use: 2D Matrix (V × V)  stores distance for every pair of nodes.
Idea: check if going through a node K gives a shorter path from i → j.

5 nodes: A,B,C,D,E. 
Starting matrix = direct edge weights:

How it calculates:
  • Build an N×N distance matrix start with direct edge weights, ∞ where no edge
  • Try every node k as an intermediate "stepping stone"
  • For every pair (i, j): check if going through k is shorterdist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])
  • Repeat for all k from 1 to N

After running Floyd-Warshall (step by step):

  • Try A as intermediate:
    → No updates, no shorter paths found
  • Try B as intermediate:
    → A→C = A→B→C = 3 + 2 = 5 ✓ (better than ∞)
    → A→D = A→B→D = 3 + 6 = 9 ✓
  • Try C as intermediate:
    → A→D = min(9, 5 + 1) = 6 ✓ (improved)
    → B→D = B→C→D = 2 + 1 = 3 ✓
  • Try D as intermediate:
    → A→E = min(7, 6 + 2) = 7 (no improvement)
    → C→E = C→D→E = 1 + 2 = 3 ✓
  • Try E as intermediate:
    → A→B = min(3, 7 + 4) = 3 (no improvement)
Final: Shortest path A→C = 5 using path A → B → C
Flow:
Init matrix with directed edges (∞ where no edge, 0 on diagonal)

k = A (try A as intermediate):
For all (i, j): dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][A] + dist[A][j])

A→C: min(∞, 3+2) = 5 ✓ UPDATE
A→D: min(∞, 3+6) = 9 ✓ UPDATE
E→C: min(8, 4+2) = 6 ✓ UPDATE
E→D: min(∞, 4+6) = 10 ✓ UPDATE

A→D: min(9, 5+1) = 6 ✓ UPDATE
B→D: min(6, 2+1) = 3 ✓ UPDATE
E→D: min(10, 6+1) = 7 ✓ UPDATE

A→E: min(7, 6+2) = 7 (no change)
C→E: min(∞, 1+2) = 3 ✓ UPDATE

items: Time: O(V³) three nested loops, one for each intermediate node K, one for source i, one for destination j.
Space: O(V²) the distance matrix stores one value per pair of nodes.

blocks.text: This makes Floyd-Warshall impractical for very large graphs (V > 1000), but perfectly fine for dense graphs or when all-pairs shortest paths are needed.
Use it when you need shortest paths between every pair of nodes, the graph is small (≤ 500 nodes), and it may have negative edges (no negative cycles).

items: Network analysis
Routing tables
Detecting negative cycles (dist[i][i] < 0)
Transitive closure
Create a V×V distance matrix. Set dist[i][i] = 0 and dist[i][j] = edge weight if the edge exists, else infinity.
For each intermediate node K (outer loop), for each source i, for each destination j: check if dist[i][K] + dist[K][j] < dist[i][j]. If yes, update.
After all three loops complete, dist[i][j] holds the shortest path from i to j.
To detect negative cycles: check if any dist[i][i] < 0.

blocks.text: NOTE:Very slow for large graphs (V³). If you only need one source, use Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford instead.
Finds the shortest path from one node to all others, even with negative weights. Slower than Dijkstra but more powerful.

It updates distances again and again (relaxation) for V-1 times until all shortest paths are found.
If one more round still updates anything → there is a negative cycle.
Data Structure to use: Array just store distances, no heap needed.
Each round improves distances step by step. After V-1 rounds, everything is correct (unless a negative cycle exists).

items: Assign distance ∞ to all nodes, 0 to source
Repeat (N-1) times for N nodes:Go through every single edge in the graphFor each edge (u→v, weight w): if dist[u] + w < dist[v] → update dist[v]
After N-1 rounds, run one more round if anything still updates, there's a negative cycle

blocks.text: Time Complexity

items: Time: O(V × E) V-1 passes, each scanning all E edges.
Space: O(V) just the distance array.

blocks.text: This is slower than Dijkstra's O((V+E) log V), which is why Dijkstra is preferred when there are no negative weights.
Use it when the graph has negative weights, when you need to detect negative cycles, or when the graph is small enough for O(V × E).

items: Currency exchange (detect profitable loops)
Network routing (RIP)
Financial graphs
Set all distances to infinity except the source (distance = 0).
Loop V-1 times. In each loop, go through every edge (u, v, w). If dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v].
After V-1 loops, run one more pass. If any distance still improves, a negative cycle exists report it.
Otherwise, return the distance array.

blocks.text: NOTE: Bellman-Ford is slower than Dijkstra. If no negative edges exist, prefer Dijkstra. If negative cycles exist, no shortest path is defined — Bellman-Ford will detect it.
